Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

According to recent reports, models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Sources indicate that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

According to recent reports, our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Sources indicate that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

In a recent development, for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

In a recent development, RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

According to recent reports, each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

Industry observers note that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Industry observers note that each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Recent findings suggest that of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below highlights how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

It has been revealed that qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

According to recent reports, this example indicates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below demonstrates what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

In a recent development, to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

In a recent development, each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Sources indicate that before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

According to recent reports, the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

In a recent development, merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

It has been revealed that we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

Industry observers note that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

In a recent development, the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own upgrade. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Sources indicate that use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

Sources indicate that the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

In a recent development, during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets upcoming tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

According to recent reports, we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

According to recent reports, every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

Sources indicate that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the owners and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

Industry observers note that this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

It has been revealed that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

According to recent reports, thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

In a recent development, nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.

What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information.
  • It’s like your computer’s hard drive.
  • In a recent development, blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

In a recent development, blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many owners and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

According to recent reports, and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more promptly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some massive-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Industry observers note that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Sources indicate that blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

In a recent development, have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

It has been revealed that blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

According to recent reports, yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of consumers constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Recent findings suggest that coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain manufacturer in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Industry observers note that blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Industry observers note that blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This post walks through the numbers, the protocols, and the parts of your stack that decide whether an AI assistant can cite your products at all.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you build or maintain an online store, you've probably been asked some version of "should we integrate checkout into ChatGPT?" this year. The honest engineering answer, based on what the platforms themselves now say, is: the integration that matters first is not checkout. It's your data.

This post walks through the numbers, the protocols, and the parts of your stack that decide whether an AI assistant can cite your products at all.

A quick note on where I'm coming from. I've worked in SEO since the beginning, in the AltaVista days, and I've watched visibility algorithms change over and over. My work has covered eCommerce retail, real estate, hospitality and startups, and I mentor founders and teams on digital exposure and their digital footprint. I try to think one step ahead and keep common sense in the loop. I'm an Event Ambassador at E-commerce Berlin Expo, where I've also spoken, and I've sat on the jury of the E-commerce Germany Awards. In February 2027 I'll be on that jury again in Germany.

In a recent development, treat these as separate measurements with different methods. They are not directly comparable.

In a recent development, the engineering takeaway from row four: open-ended prompts ("lightweight running shoes for flat feet") trigger shopping about four times as often as brand-named ones. [4] The model picks products when the user doesn't. That selection runs on whatever data it can parse.

Two open protocols are worth knowing.

Sources indicate that agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP). OpenAI and Stripe released it on 29 September 2025 alongside Instant Checkout, starting with U.S. Etsy sellers. [9] The merchant stays merchant of record; orders, payments and fulfillment run through the merchant's existing systems. [9] OpenAI's merchant page now describes ACP as supporting "product discovery and more accurate, personalized recommendations through shared product data", and indicates it is "moving away from a standalone Instant Checkout experience", with purchases completed on merchant websites or apps. [8].

Industry observers note that universal Commerce Protocol (UCP). Google announced it on 11 January 2026, co-developed with Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target and Walmart. It is meant to power checkout on eligible listings in AI Mode in Search and the Gemini app, with the retailer remaining seller of record. [10].

So the pattern in late 2026: the agent protocols exist, but in ChatGPT the live value is discovery from shared product data, and the transaction lands on your site. If you're prioritizing work, feed quality comes before checkout plumbing.

Sources indicate that the platforms spell this out. OpenAI invites merchants to share product feeds and says richer, up-to-date data helps products surface with more accurate information. It also says a feed isn't required if ChatGPT already crawls your site, but feeds give more control. [8] Shopify generates a catalog for AI channels automatically and lists what helps: clear titles, full-sentence descriptions, technical details, sizing and care information, public return policies, and reviews. [7].

A practical checklist for the catalog:.

Sources indicate that I call the resulting dynamic the Citation Economy, a term I coined: search made us compete for clicks, AI makes us compete for citations. The path is cited, compared, chosen, bought. Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), making pages and product data easy for AI assistants to read, trust and cite, is just SEO with a new reader: the model.

A hypothetical German online jewelry shop gets this kind of request through an assistant: a minimalist gold necklace, hypoallergenic, within a budget, delivered before a birthday. No brand named.

According to recent reports, A product record that only carries title: "Necklace gold" gives the model nothing to match. One that states metal, plating, allergy information, delivery time and return policy can be matched to every constraint in the prompt, and to the follow-up ("which is better for sensitive skin?") if that answer is on the page. Same product, very different odds of being cited.

Shopify recommends tracking AI referrals separately from organic search, using custom filters or reports in GA4. [7] A simple starting point is a custom channel group or exploration filter on session source matching the assistants' referrer domains, for example chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai and gemini.google.com. Then compare conversion rate and revenue per session against organic search.

Sources indicate that add one manual step: once a month, ask the assistants your key buyer questions by hand and log whether your products are cited. ChatGPT's shopping features are U.S.-only for now [8], so test in the markets you actually sell in.

OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT in the U.S. on 9 February 2026, matched to conversation topic, and says ads don't influence answers. [11] It added CPC bidding and a self-serve Ads Manager in May 2026 [12], and in September 2026 debuted a ChatGPT Ads app for U.S. Shopify merchants plus a Sponsored Agents test. [13] Ads sit next to the answer. Getting cited is still how you get into it.

According to recent reports, for developers the useful reframe is this: AI shopping in 2026 is less an integration project and more a data-quality project. Ship clean, complete, consistent product data, publish the answers shoppers ask for, and instrument AI referrals as a first-class channel. Checkout can follow when the platforms and your numbers say it's worth it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pixelvile started on a PC I borrowed from my uncle.
  • It has been revealed that today we're a small team in Kolkata, India.
  • We started with games on Steam and Roblox, then worked behind the scenes as subcontractors for other studios.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pixelvile started on a PC I borrowed from my uncle. It switched off every 10 minutes, so I learned to save after every few lines of code. A year later he took it back. By then the work it made possible had paid for a proper laptop.

It has been revealed that today we're a small team in Kolkata, India. We've done roughly 1,000 projects for 600+ clients: games, web apps, SaaS platforms and websites. Here's what that taught us, especially about building for small businesses.

We started with games on Steam and Roblox, then worked behind the scenes as subcontractors for other studios. Many of those projects still run today under other names.

Sources indicate that none of it was glamorous. Bug fixes, small scripts, quick sites. But small jobs pay the next month's bills, and every one of them shows you a real problem someone was willing to pay to fix.

A typical local business, say a clinic, a salon or a café, runs on four tools that don't talk to each other: a website, a booking app, a spreadsheet of customers, and an invoicing app. Four logins, four bills, and nothing connects.

So we built one dashboard that does all four: the website, online booking, customer records, staff calendars, invoices and stock. We set it up for each business and look after it every month.

The hard part wasn't the code. It was making it simple enough for an owner who checks everything on their phone between customers.

Building for local businesses in India taught us things no feature list would:.

Most missed appointments aren't rude. People are busy and they forget. One reminder the day before, with a one-tap way to change the time, fixes most of them. For long or high-value slots, a small advance via UPI helps even more.

The most common questions we get from businesses leaving another agency:.

Recent findings suggest that we put the opposite in writing: if a client leaves, they take their domain, their content and a full export of their customer data. Lock-in feels like a moat, but it's really a reason nobody refers you.

A site with no booking, no updates and the domain registered in the agency's name costs you twice: once to build it, and again to escape it. Before paying anyone for a website, ask three questions:.

Sources indicate that for years almost all our clients found us online, paid through PayPal, and never met us. Now we're doing the opposite: walking into local cafés and clinics in Kolkata. It's harder, and a lot more fun.

If you're building for small businesses too, I'd love to hear what surprised you. And if you want to see what we've built, there's a demo dashboard you can open without signing up at pixelvile.com/demos.

  • Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
  • An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.
  • Recent findings suggest that affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Recent findings suggest that affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Sources indicate that performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Sources indicate that smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a massive opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

It has been revealed that A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Sources indicate that because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:.

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:.

Recent findings suggest that commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#46448. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2446 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model.
  • Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly fresh great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

It has been revealed that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

It has been revealed that in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

Sources indicate that pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

In a recent development, available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

According to recent reports, SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

It has been revealed that MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Over the Still Sea (Qwen 3.8 27B).

Sources indicate that build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

It has been revealed that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Industry observers note that inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

Sources indicate that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

It has been revealed that we ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. On November 16, 2026, researcher Xusheng Li published a reverse-engineering write-up of a Windows 11 component that can record which coding agents and developer tools ran on a PC.

It has been revealed that the report he captured is a daily seen bitmap of matching executable names, not a log of prompts or source code. The work is one researcher's reverse engineering, and the feature has not been shown to be active on every Windows 11 install.

In a recent development, optional diagnostic data was already on in the US Windows 11 Home test he ran. Microsoft's diagnostics page claims you choose that setting when you set up the device. I could not find a public Microsoft response as of November 17, 2026.

The Hacker News thread had 661 points and 519 comments as of 1:46 PM Europe/London on November 17, 2026. I am going by Li's post, not a test I ran on my own machine.

Recent findings suggest that li started from executable names embedded in MissionControlAggregator.dll, including claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and copilot.exe. The feature that gates the new agent checks is named CLICodingAgentUsage.

In a recent development, the match list is longer than those four names. Four CLI-agent slots check copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, plus extensionless equivalents on the WSL path. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.

The same component also groups ordinary developer tools, such as python.exe, node.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, into twelve broader categories.

Industry observers note that li tested a Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974, where the feature was already enabled as a service experiment, and a clean US Windows 11 Home ARM64 install for the diagnostic-data default. A service experiment is not the same thing as a setting that is on for every install.

Industry observers note that secondary recaps followed on November 17. They restate Li's findings, and none of the ones I found reports an independent reproduction.

The six checks below are my structure, drawn from Li's write-up and Microsoft's diagnostics page, not a list Microsoft published.

The agent-usage report Li captured was marked optional, not required ("isRequired": false). On a clean install of Windows 11 Home ARM64 with the region set to the United States, he found the Diagnostic data toggle already enabled and labeled Include Optional, and AllowTelemetry set to 3.

He did not test other regions. Microsoft's support page describes optional diagnostic data as extra detail about the device, and says it may include websites browsed, device activity (sometimes called usage), and enhanced error reporting.

Microsoft also says it collects some optional data from only a sample of devices, and the Diagnostic Data Viewer shows whether a device is in that sample.

The same guide also states: "When you set up your Windows device for the first time, you can choose to send optional diagnostic data to Microsoft." The page does not name this aggregator or coding agents, and the text I opened does not state a single worldwide default.

Check whether Send optional diagnostic data is still on under Settings, Privacy & security, Diagnostics & feedback.

DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was running Automatic on Li's VM. The service started AggregatorHost.exe, and that child process loaded MissionControlAggregator.dll.

It has been revealed that CLICodingAgentUsage was already on as a service experiment. He had not turned it on himself. A blog post about one VM is not proof that the same component is loaded on this PC.

In a recent development, li describes the process and DLL he observed. From an admin prompt, tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll shows whether AggregatorHost.exe has the DLL loaded, which is the check Li ran.

The match list is broader than the four best-known agents. The CLI slots include agy.exe. The desktop slots include antigravity.exe and github.exe. Everyday tools sit in twelve categories.

WSL exec events can also feed the CLI matchers, and a normal Windows codex.exe can reach those matchers through the app-state summary path. Some tool checks also compare a publisher name. The GCC and Clang group does not, on the path Li describes.

If the feature is on, check which tools on this machine could turn on a bit.

In a recent development, the report is named Segments.SubCohorts (event Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts, version 0.1.5 in his capture). ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns matches into bits for twelve tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

An on Codex bit means a matching name was seen in the window. The bit does not mean Microsoft received prompts, source, or how long the tool ran. Li indicates the source events contain runtime and focus data, and that this component appears to discard those details.

He found no prompt text or source code in the report. The window is roughly daily. The honest description is a usage bitmap, not a keylogger.

Industry observers note that li copied cmd.exe to codex.exe and ran it. The name alone turned on the Codex CLI bit. A gcc.exe copy turned on the shared compiler and debugger category, not a unique GCC bit.

Sources indicate that microsoft's public diagnostics page explains required versus optional data and the Settings path. It has been revealed that no Microsoft comment on the finding was found on November 17, 2026. The review questions are whether this is a personal device you can reconfigure, or a managed one, and whether Microsoft has said anything newly introduced since the post.

The post does not show that Microsoft is collecting prompts or source code in this report. The post does not show that every Windows 11 install is uploading agent-usage bits.

Turning off optional diagnostic data is the opt-out Li describes for this report. The switch is broader than coding agents alone. Privacy concerns about a seen bitmap of developer tools are still real, and they should be stated without inflating the evidence.

Microsoft's Diagnostic Data Viewer, linked from the same Settings page, is the official way to look at what a PC is sending. The viewer shows events in real time while it runs, not a history.

#46443. Latest Update: ZGC vs G1: Trading CPU for Pause-Free Memory Reclamation

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1006 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: ZGC vs G1: Trading CPU for Pause-Free Memory Reclamation

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A Java service that caches a few million objects eventually has to throw them away, and how it does so determines whether users see a smooth response time or a periodic freeze.
  • G1 keeps pause times in the tens of milliseconds by collecting in small region increments, while ZGC keeps them under a millisecond regardless of heap size by doing the compaction work concurrently with the application — the price is extra CPU and heap headroom.
  • According to recent reports, the decision is not about which collector is newer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Java service that caches a few million objects eventually has to throw them away, and how it does so determines whether users see a smooth response time or a periodic freeze. For years the default collector was G1, which broke the heap into regions and cleaned a few at a time to keep pauses short. ZGC changed the bargain: it moves objects while the program is still running, so even a heap measured in terabytes pauses for roughly the time it takes to stop the threads at a safepoint.

G1 keeps pause times in the tens of milliseconds by collecting in small region increments, while ZGC keeps them under a millisecond regardless of heap size by doing the compaction work concurrently with the application — the price is extra CPU and heap headroom.

According to recent reports, the decision is not about which collector is newer. It is about what you are willing to spend to remove a specific kind of latency, because both collectors eventually reclaim the same garbage and both keep the program correct.

According to recent reports, G1 treats the heap as a set of equal-sized regions and maintains a list of which ones are mostly garbage. It collects the cheapest regions first, and it can pause the application to move the surviving objects of a few regions into fresh ones. That pause is proportional to the number of regions it handles in one cycle, which the collector can bound with a pause target. Set a 50 millisecond goal and G1 will try to do only enough work per cycle to hit it, leaving the rest for later.

Recent findings suggest that the consequence is that G1 pauses grow with the amount of live data it must evacuate in a cycle. Under a large, long-lived cache, the regions it picks contain more survivors, each cycle has more copying to do, and meeting a tight target gets harder. G1 also needs a remembered set per region to track references from elsewhere, and those structures consume memory and CPU on every write.

A ZGC cycle uses coloured pointers and load barriers to relocate objects while application threads keep running, so its pause is a safepoint of well under a millisecond — but the load barrier touches every reference read and the collector needs roughly 15 to 30 percent heap headroom to stay ahead of allocation.

ZGC takes a different route. It encodes metadata in the pointer bits themselves, using coloured pointers to mark whether an object has been moved, and it intercepts reference loads with a barrier that forwards the program to the latest location. Because the program never sees a stale pointer, the collector can relocate objects concurrently with normal execution. Only a tiny phase at the start and end of a cycle needs to stop the threads, and that stop does not scale with heap size.

In a recent development, the mechanism has a cost on every access. A load barrier is a few extra instructions on each reference read, and in pointer-heavy workloads the cumulative overhead can reach single-digit to low double-digit percentages of throughput. ZGC also needs spare memory: it cannot compact into a full heap, so it relies on headroom and on allocating into a new region while the old one is being emptied. Give it too little and it will stall the application just like any other collector.

According to recent reports, where this shows up in ordinary life is the page that takes a second to load at the same moment every afternoon. A batch job finishes, the young generation fills, G1 pauses to evacuate, and the request queue backs up for a few dozen milliseconds. Customers do not know about garbage collection, but they feel the pause as a spinner. A trading dashboard or a checkout flow is exactly where that spinner becomes a lost order.

Sources indicate that the comparison also depends on how much memory a machine has. On a service with a two gigabyte heap, G1 is easy to tune and its pauses are already small enough that nobody notices. On a fifty gigabyte in-memory index, the same pause target forces G1 into a losing race with allocation, while ZGC keeps the pause flat and simply asks for more RAM and CPU.

Choose G1 when pauses in the tens of milliseconds are invisible and you want predictable throughput from modest hardware; choose ZGC when a sub-millisecond tail matters more than the CPU and memory you will spend to get it — the collector is a budget decision, not a ranking.

In a recent development, for a small service, the practical advice is to stay with the default and measure before changing anything. Turning on ZGC without a latency problem just moves cost from a rare pause into every reference read. For a latency-critical service with a large heap, the opposite is true: the steady tax is worth paying to delete the tail.

The deeper lesson is that garbage collectors trade one kind of cost for another. G1 spreads the cost into occasional stops; ZGC spreads it into continuous small overheads. Neither removes the work of reclaiming memory, so the question is always where you would rather pay it.

It has been revealed that the JVM runs a large share of enterprise backend services, and server-side Java deployments are commonly counted in the tens of millions of instances worldwide. Even if a fraction of those adopt low-latency collectors for latency-sensitive tiers, the extra memory headroom ZGC asks for translates into meaningful additional RAM per instance — a purchase decision measured in millions of servers rather than a theoretical preference.

These are order-of-magnitude estimates from published adoption ranges and stated assumptions, not a forecast for any vendor.

G1 caps pauses by collecting young regions incrementally; ZGC moves objects concurrently and keeps pauses flat even at multi-terabyte heaps — at a CPU and memory tax.

It has been revealed that if you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers.

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

According to recent reports, when you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

It has been revealed that acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include massive brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and manufacturer-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

It has been revealed that marketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool reveals you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for upcoming content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

In a recent development, copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

According to recent reports, yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert upcoming shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

According to recent reports, there are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, latest marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. #46439. RDMA vs Kernel TCP: Bypassing the Stack to Buy Lower Latency

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (902 w)
